paper_summary: A literature/patent review (Modern Applied Science, 2015) of binding agents for syntactic foams - hollow-microsphere-filled composites - used as heat-insulating coatings on power-industry pipelines and equipment. It surveys patents combining glass, ceramic, polymer and fly-ash microspheres with acrylic latex, epoxy, polyurethane, silicone, liquid-glass, phosphate and cement binders, and tabulates the qualitative characteristics and thermal stability limits of thermoset, thermoplastic and inorganic binder classes. It concludes that organic/element-organic binders are limited to about 400 C while phosphate and aluminosilicate binders (stable to ~2000 C) are the most promising but under-studied.

extraction_notes: This is a REVIEW/patent survey; the authors report no measurements of their own. Every record is therefore data_origin='secondary', with the source patent or paper named in sample_label. Only rows of Table 1 and passages of Sec. 4 that state a numeric property were turned into records; Table 1 rows with purely qualitative outcomes (modified ash microspheres/polyurethane, latex-composite coating, epoxy 'high adhesion to a pipe', Lestosil silicone/boron nitride, metallised ceramic microspheres) were skipped, as were Tables 2 and 3, which describe binder chemistry and setting behaviour rather than foam properties. Many quoted properties are ranges (0.02-0.03, 0.16-0.175, 0.029-0.034 W/(m*K); 51-75 kg/m^3); those fields are left null with the range recorded in microstructure_notes, per the no-invented-numbers rule. Values stated as 'up to X' are recorded as X with a note. Unit conversions: breaking strength 2.4 kgf/mm^2 -> 23.5 MPa (x 9.80665); densities kg/m^3 -> g/cm^3 (51 -> 0.051, 400 -> 0.4, 600 -> 0.6). The '51kg/mm3' in Table 1 is a typographic error for 51 kg/m^3. Process route, particle size, particle loading, test standards, strain rates and test temperatures are not given for any composition, so those fields are null; process_route='other' throughout. Maximum service temperatures quoted in Table 1 (150 C, 600-650 C) are operating limits, not test temperatures, so they are kept in notes rather than test.temperature_c. Confidence is low-to-moderate on all records because they are unverified patent/advertising claims - the paper itself criticises the 0.001 W/(m*K) figure as unrealistic.
